KEY MESSAGE 1...

Latest satellite imagery shows a vertically stacked cut-off low
in the Ohio Valley, approaching shortwave into the Great Lakes 
and strong ridging off shore supporting a deep fetch moisture 
from the Gulf and western Atlantic up the East Coast. This
meridionally flow pattern will result in a highly moisture rich
and humid environment across the Northeast through tomorrow as 
anomalously strong V-wind components allow PWATs to surge 
impressively towards 2-2.25" or 3 standard deviations above 
normal per the ENS standard anomalies. As the northern stream
shortwave tracks into the Great Lakes today, it looks to slow
down as it interacts with the closed low and amplify as it takes
on a negative tilt through tonight. With this shortwave displaced
well to our west and weak subsidence still overhead from the 
off shore ridge, the moisture and heavy rain axis looks to be 
focused more in the Saint Lawrence River Valley and southern 
Canada most of today. However, as the leading edge of the low 
and mid-level southerly jet and impressive PWAT plume noses 
into the Northeast late this morning into the afternoon, high 
res guidance shows a few scattered showers and weak 
thunderstorms tracking into the southwest Adirondacks and 
western Mohawk Vally. Warm/moist mid-levels will keep lapse 
rates poor, limit instability and therefore likely prevent any 
severe storms.

The heavy rain/moisture axis from the Saint Lawrence River
Valley shifts eastward tonight into eastern NY and western New
England as the northern stream trough takes on a negative tilt.
The favorable overlap of strong forcing for ascent, weak 
instability and strengthening southerly flow through a deep 
layer within a highly moisture rich environment will support 
high rainfall rates. The latest PMM from the HREF shows a 30 - 
50% chance for over 1" of rain in 3hrs and even a small area 
with a 10% chance of over 3" of rain in 3hrs during the 06 - 15 
UTC Monday window. The highest probabilities and QPF maxima 
areas are favored in the mid-Hudson Valley into western MA and 
NW CT, similar to the slight risk Day 2 ERO placement. While 
bands of heavy rain should be rather progressive, the 
unidirectional flow through a deep layer suggest potential for 
heavy rain to repeatedly impact a given area tonight into Monday
morning. With 1hr and 3hr flash flood guidance values generally
1.75 - 2.5" here, it will take repeatedly rounds of heavy rain 
to raise concerns for isolated to scattered flash flooding; 
however, the impressive moisture anomalies and favorable warm 
rain processes supporting high rainfall rates means we will 
need to closely monitor rainfall trends overnight into Monday 
morning.

The main moisture/heavy rain axis shifts into New England 
Monday morning as the parent shortwave cuts-off and pushes
eastward. However, there is increasing confidence for a line of
strong to even severe storms to develop ahead of the sfc
boundary as it tracks eastward Monday afternoon. Storms can
certainly produce additional heavy downpours as instability
increases on Monday and any areas that become saturated from 
the overnight/Monday A.M rain will be vulnerable to additional 
localized flooding. Between 8PM Sun and 8PM Mon, the latest NBM
probabilistic guidance still shows a 40 to 70% chance for 24hr 
rainfall amounts to exceed 1" with even a 20 to 35% chance for
over 2". The highest probabilities are favored in the Day 2 ERO
slight risk (level 2 of 4) area in the mid-Hudson Valley and NW
CT; however, these areas mainly missed out on the record 
rainfall last week so decided to hold off on a Flood Watch in 
collaboration with neighboring WFOs. A marginal risk (level 1 of
4) in the Day 2 ERO extends further north/west into most of
eastern NY where any flash flooding should be isolated. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...

After the main area of rain exits into New England Monday 
morning, there may be a brief opportunity for filtered sun to 
help destabilize the atmosphere before the main trough axis 
swings through the region Monday afternoon. The best chance for
this looks to be from the Capital District/Upper Hudson Valley
eastward into western New England where there will be a few hour
delay between the exiting morning rain and the sfc boundary.
Given the high dew points/very humid air mass in place, any
insolation will quickly increase sfc based instability. However,
forecast soundings show a rather moist column so mid-level lapse
rates are rather poor. Even still, the fast flow aloft and a 
veering wind profile in the low-levels will support both 
directional and speed shear with 0-6km shear values nearing
40kts. This regime looks to favor wet microbursts leading to
localized damaging winds from any storms that can grow upscale 
with sustained updrafts. SPC expanded the marginal risk in its 
Day 2 Outlook to message damaging wind potential from any severe
